articles.author: calvin-rook
articles.title: The PSPN awards ballots: six writers, thirty-six choices
articles.dek: Marino leads the MVP debate, the rookie ballots spread across several clubs, and the staff explains every regular-season choice.

body.text: These are PSPN editorial ballots for the completed regular season, submitted by Mara Voss, Ellis Quill, Dorian Pike, Rowan Vale, Tessa Wren and Calvin Rook. They are our selections, preserved before the game’s eventual official awards. They do not represent fan, player or coach voting. Rookie eligibility follows the league’s first-season designation; every rookie chosen here has at least ten recorded appearances.
Mara Voss
MVP: Dram Marino — Mossdeep Eclipse

Dram Marino threw fifty-six touchdowns and four interceptions on 374 attempts. I am not treating his planned rest in the final two games as a weakness in that season. He produced 4,341 yards, sustained the league’s highest-scoring offense and left Mossdeep able to use the closing weeks for development. Manning led in yards; Marino did far more scoring with fewer attempts and fewer mistakes.
Offensive Player of the Year: Accel BeckhmJr — Mossdeep Eclipse

Accel BeckhmJr finished with 1,953 receiving yards and thirty-two receiving touchdowns on seventy-nine catches. He supplied a long gain or a score often enough to change what the defense had to protect. HeeDee Lamb’s ninety-five catches and 1,878 yards deserve a serious argument. Accel’s fourteen-touchdown advantage in receiving production decides mine.
Defensive Player of the Year: NeMarcus Tare — Saffron Psi Corps

NeMarcus Tare’s twenty-nine sacks came in thirteen appearances. The six-sack finale is a striking example, but the whole season supports the ballot. He also recorded sixty-five pressures, twelve passes defended and an interception. Chen Norton Jr’s twenty-three sacks help explain why the protection could not simply devote every answer to Tare; that partnership does not erase the individual finishing work.
Offensive Rookie of the Year: Ponyta — Veilstone Fists

Veilstone’s Ponyta led the eligible rookies here with 750 receiving yards and five receiving touchdowns. Forty-eight catches in fifteen appearances gave an inconsistent offense usable production. Wugtrio’s seven touchdowns are attractive, but the 174-yard difference and Ponyta’s broader receiving workload make this my choice.
Defensive Rookie of the Year: Volbeat — Mauville Dynamos

Mauville’s Volbeat produced thirteen sacks, seven tackles for loss and forty-three tackles in fifteen games. I value that repeated disruption over a rookie ballot decided only by an interception total. Toedscruel and Tatsugiri have strong coverage cases. Volbeat made enough opposing possessions harder to earn this vote.
Coach of the Year: Michael Dorrill — Mossdeep Eclipse

Michael Dorrill finished 17–0 with 724 points scored and 130 allowed, then used the final weeks to give younger players meaningful work while resting starters. The available evidence supports both winning and preparation. I do not need an invented preseason expectation to recognize the achievement. The demands remain exacting because the team has earned a championship opportunity.
Ellis Quill
MVP: Dram Marino — Mossdeep Eclipse

Marino’s fifty-six touchdowns and four interceptions make the clearest individual case. I also value how his season allowed Mossdeep to prepare beyond the immediate starting group. His planned late rest followed fifteen appearances of extraordinary production. The award is for the regular season that was completed, and that season does not become smaller because the coach could afford to give the next quarterback work.
Offensive Player of the Year: Garshawn Lynch — Mt. Silver Reds

Garshawn Lynch led the league with 1,200 rushing yards in eleven appearances and added 292 receiving yards. Mt. Silver’s passing personnel changed repeatedly, and his running remained a way to organize an offense through that disruption. Accel’s receiving season is larger by the most obvious scoring measure. I am choosing the sustained importance of Lynch’s work to a team that needed it in several different circumstances.
Defensive Player of the Year: NeMarcus Tare — Saffron Psi Corps

Tare’s twenty-nine sacks are the strongest finishing total. Thirteen appearances make the achievement more concentrated rather than less real. His pressure helped a Saffron defense that conceded 138 points, and he added an interception and twelve passes defended. Matthews’ broader disruption deserves discussion, but I cannot move past the repeated possessions Tare ended behind the line.
Offensive Rookie of the Year: Vigoroth — Veilstone Fists

Veilstone’s Vigoroth rushed for 807 yards in twelve appearances, the largest rushing total among the eligible rookies considered here. Three touchdowns do not capture all the ordinary work needed to keep an offense moving. Ponyta has the stronger receiving case, even on the same club. I give this ballot to the runner whose workload and yardage repeatedly provided a foundation.
Defensive Rookie of the Year: Tatsugiri — Cinnabar Blaze

Cinnabar’s Tatsugiri played all seventeen games, recorded eighty-one tackles, intercepted five passes and defended thirteen. That is a substantial full-season responsibility for a rookie safety. Volbeat’s sacks offer more immediate disruption, but I value the volume and continuity of the defensive work that helped a twelve-win club finish its schedule.
Coach of the Year: Travis Scarboro — Lavender Wails

Travis Scarboro took a 4–5 team through eight consecutive wins and a division championship while replacing an injured passing option. The ending was dramatic, but the ballot covers the whole recovery. Lavender had to keep functioning through close games and changes in responsibility. Scarboro’s team continued to find enough useful answers to make the final kick matter.
Dorian Pike
MVP: Garshawn Lynch — Mt. Silver Reds

Garshawn Lynch: 1,200 rushing yards on 155 carries, fifteen combined rushing and receiving touchdowns, eleven appearances. Mt. Silver lost quarterbacks and targets and still finished 14–3 with the conference’s first seed. Marino has the obvious statistical case. I am voting for the player who kept giving an injured contender a way to impose its own game. This is a value judgment, and I am putting my name beside it.
Offensive Player of the Year: HeeDee Lamb — Saffron Psi Corps

HeeDee Lamb caught ninety-five passes for 1,878 yards and eighteen touchdowns, then added 177 rushing yards, three rushing touchdowns and a passing touchdown. Accel has more receiving yards and many more receiving scores. Lamb’s range of offensive work and full seventeen-game contribution earn my ballot. I expect Mara to read me the thirty-two-touchdown number again; I have read it.
Defensive Player of the Year: Blayz Matthews — Mt. Silver Reds

Blayz Matthews had 17.5 sacks, sixteen tackles for loss and seventy pressures over seventeen games. Tare wins the sack comparison emphatically. Matthews wins my vote for the wider, season-long disruption, including the work that stopped a runner before the line and the pressure that did not finish as a sack. Mt. Silver’s defense needed that repeated contribution while the offense changed around it.
Offensive Rookie of the Year: Wugtrio — Mauville Dynamos

Mauville’s Wugtrio scored seven receiving touchdowns, the most persuasive finishing number in this rookie receiving debate. The 576 yards trail Ponyta and Dragonair, and I am accepting that tradeoff. Thirty-seven catches produced seven scores. The Dynamos did not reach the playoffs, but the rookie repeatedly completed the part of the offensive possession that changes the scoreboard.
Defensive Rookie of the Year: Toedscruel — Petalburg Pride

Petalburg’s Toedscruel intercepted five passes and defended fifteen in sixteen appearances. The Pride won twelve games with very little spare scoring margin across the season. I value the rookie who helped make those defensive possessions useful. Tatsugiri has more tackles, Volbeat more sacks; Toedscruel’s coverage production gets my choice.
Coach of the Year: Connor McLarren — Mt. Silver Reds

Connor McLarren kept Mt. Silver at the top of Kanto–Johto through repeated quarterback and receiving injuries. Fourteen wins and a bye are tangible results. The finale was poor, and the injury list remains ugly. A regular-season coaching ballot should still account for the team continuing to win while the available offense kept changing. I give McLarren that credit.
Rowan Vale
MVP: Archam Manning — Saffron Psi Corps

Archam Manning led the league with 4,633 passing yards, threw forty-three touchdowns and started all seventeen games for a 14–3 team. Marino’s efficiency is better; I am choosing the full-season offensive burden carried by Manning. Saffron finished with 597 points and three narrow defeats. The quarterback kept its scoring threat present every week, including a five-touchdown finale.
Offensive Player of the Year: Accel BeckhmJr — Mossdeep Eclipse

Thirty-two receiving touchdowns. I can put other numbers around Accel BeckhmJr’s season, including 1,953 yards and seventy-nine catches, but the finishing total does most of the work. Lamb was spectacular and more versatile. Accel’s receiving production repeatedly turned a productive Mossdeep drive into seven points before the defense had time to enjoy its previous successful snap.
Defensive Player of the Year: NeMarcus Tare — Saffron Psi Corps

Tare finished with twenty-nine sacks, six more than the next player, and added sixty-five pressures. He missed some appearances and still led the league. I enjoy Matthews’ seventy pressures and sixteen tackles for loss, but I am taking the defender who most often completed the pass rush with the quarterback on the ground.
Offensive Rookie of the Year: Ponyta — Veilstone Fists

Ponyta produced 750 receiving yards and five touchdowns in fifteen games. Dragonair was fifteen yards behind with two fewer scores; Wugtrio had two more scores but substantially fewer yards. I give the Veilstone receiver the best combination of production and finishing among those three. The team’s six wins do not make the rookie’s catches disappear.
Defensive Rookie of the Year: Volbeat — Mauville Dynamos

Thirteen sacks from Mauville’s Volbeat are a substantial rookie season, with seven tackles for loss and forty-three tackles alongside them. I prefer the repeated backfield disruption to deciding this ballot on five interceptions shared by two other candidates. The Dynamos missed the field; Volbeat still supplied an individual season worth honoring.
Coach of the Year: Michael Dorrill — Mossdeep Eclipse

Michael Dorrill won seventeen games, including the two in which he deliberately gave younger players larger jobs. A 594-point differential gives me no reason to invent a more dramatic regular-season coaching result. The team is expected to win now because it has kept winning. Dorrill helped create that expectation and then continued to meet it.
Tessa Wren
MVP: Dram Marino — Mossdeep Eclipse

Marino combined 4,341 passing yards, fifty-six touchdowns and four interceptions with a 17–0 team result. His fifteen appearances reflect the late rest plan, not a failed attempt to remain productive. Manning’s larger yardage total came on 134 more attempts. I favor Marino’s efficiency, scoring production and control of mistakes.
Offensive Player of the Year: Accel BeckhmJr — Mossdeep Eclipse

Accel’s 1,953 receiving yards and thirty-two touchdowns put him ahead of the other offensive candidates on my ballot. Ninjaskamara’s twenty rushing touchdowns and Lamb’s broader duties deserve recognition, but the receiver’s ability to finish from a productive target share gives Mossdeep the clearest individual offensive honor.
Defensive Player of the Year: NeMarcus Tare — Saffron Psi Corps

Tare’s twenty-nine sacks lead a strong group, with sixty-five pressures and five tackles for loss supporting the case. Norton had twenty-three sacks and sixty-six pressures, so this is a close look at two teammates rather than a claim that Tare worked alone. The six-sack advantage decides my vote.
Offensive Rookie of the Year: Ponyta — Veilstone Fists

Ponyta’s forty-eight catches, 750 yards and five touchdowns are the most balanced receiving case among the eligible rookies. Vigoroth had more rushing yards and Wugtrio more receiving touchdowns. I prefer the combination of a substantial receiving workload and five finishes across fifteen appearances.
Defensive Rookie of the Year: Toedscruel — Petalburg Pride

Toedscruel’s five interceptions and fifteen passes defended came in sixteen games for Petalburg. Tatsugiri also had five interceptions, with more tackles and two fewer passes defended. I choose the cornerback’s coverage production, while treating that comparison as an editorial judgment rather than pretending the available totals measure every coverage assignment.
Coach of the Year: Gardenia — Eterna Thorns

Gardenia won eleven games with an offense that scored 214 points and a defense that allowed 184. Eterna beat Sunyshore and Petalburg and earned a home playoff game. Dorrill’s perfect season is the strongest alternative. My ballot recognizes how consistently Gardenia’s team made a restricted scoring range sufficient to win.
Calvin Rook
MVP: Dram Marino — Mossdeep Eclipse

Marino’s fifty-six touchdown passes against four interceptions are the cleanest evidence of a quarterback converting his opportunities into exceptional production. The 4,341 yards came on 374 attempts. From a scouting perspective, the important part is how repeatedly the offense turned his strengths into useful work, not an imagined ceiling. The season supplies the result.
Offensive Player of the Year: Accel BeckhmJr — Mossdeep Eclipse

Accel BeckhmJr finished with 1,953 receiving yards and thirty-two touchdowns. I look for a player whose specific job produces an advantage the opponent repeatedly fails to remove. This receiving season provides that evidence. Lamb’s versatility is attractive, but Accel’s established work as a receiver is enough to lead the ballot without borrowing credit from a different role.
Defensive Player of the Year: NeMarcus Tare — Saffron Psi Corps

Tare’s twenty-nine sacks in thirteen games give him the strongest case. Sixty-five pressures, twelve passes defended and an interception broaden it. Matthews and Norton show how different disruption profiles can be valuable. I choose Tare because the available season records show the most frequent completed pass-rush impact, while recognizing the teammates who made the defensive structure work.
Offensive Rookie of the Year: Dragonair — Viridian Titans

Viridian’s Dragonair caught forty-six passes for 735 yards across all seventeen games. Ponyta had fifteen more yards and two more touchdowns in fewer appearances, so that is the stronger efficiency alternative. I give Dragonair a narrow vote for the full-season workload and the ability to remain a useful receiving option in a five-win offense. This is a scouting-informed preference grounded in actual work, not a prediction of future growth.
Defensive Rookie of the Year: Thievul — Cinnabar Blaze

Cinnabar’s Thievul defended twenty-three passes, intercepted two and made thirty-seven tackles in sixteen games. The lower interception total will cost him some ballots. I value the repeated pass-defense contribution enough to choose him over the more spectacular sack and interception leaders. The available record does not supply a complete coverage grade, so this remains a considered editorial choice.
Coach of the Year: Michael Dorrill — Mossdeep Eclipse

Dorrill paired seventeen wins with deliberate late-season experience for younger players. Budew Baker’s two starts produced five touchdown passes and two victories while the established offense rested. Development matters when it occurs inside useful jobs and the team still accomplishes its immediate task. That combination strengthens an already exceptional regular-season coaching case.
